name: Huang-lien-chieh-tu-tang (oren-gedoku-to, huanglian-jie-du-tang)
short: Mesenteric phlebosclerosis (colon disease): 1 case; 4 of 25 cases used it for years. Less platelet clumping in 10 stroke patients. Pneumonitis: 2 cases. Scutellaria-root formulas: lung, liver harm.
text: Names: the page's 1983 case report calls this formula a traditional kanpo medicine, Huang-lien-chieh-tu-tang; other abstracts give the Kampo name oren-gedoku-to with the Chinese name huanglian-jie-du-tang, describe it as a prescription medicine in Japan, China and Korea, and say it has four constituent herbs; one of them, Scutellaria root, is called ougon (also spelled ogon) in Japanese. No cited abstract links the spelling Huang-lien-chieh-tu-tang directly to oren-gedoku-to; the page lists them as one formula. Lung injury (case report): a 54-year-old man developed a high fever from the day he started oren-gedoku-to, stopped it at day 17 because of malaise and chills, and was admitted with suspected drug-induced pneumonitis; after all drugs were stopped, his symptoms, laboratory results and chest X-ray markedly improved. A lymphocyte stimulation test was positive for the formula and for one of its components, ougon (Baikal skullcap, Scutellaria root), and the authors diagnosed pneumonitis caused by ougon. A 1999 case report describes a 62-year-old man who had fever and dry cough after taking Ouren-gedoku-to for 2 months, made worse by a 5-day course of another Kampo formula, Sho-saiko-to, with ground-glass changes in both lower lungs; his clinical and X-ray findings improved after both were stopped, lymphocyte stimulation tests were negative but challenge tests with each formula were positive, and the authors suggest the involvement of ougon, the only ingredient the two share. Liver and lung injury with Scutellaria root (evidence about a group of Kampo formulas, not this formula by name): a 2022 review states that many cases of interstitial pneumonia, liver injury and allergic cystitis linked to Kampo formulas have been reported to be caused by formulas containing Scutellaria root. Japanese national reports from 2003 to 2018 listed 4,232 adverse events with prescription Kampo formulas, including 1,193 related to liver injury and 1,177 to lung injury, and about 70% of the liver and lung events were suspected to be caused by formulas containing Scutellaria root; these are reports to a national database, which cannot show how often such harm occurs. A 2017 review of 73 people with pneumonitis from Japanese herbal medicines (the abstract does not name this formula; it says the formulas used most often commonly contain ougon, Scutellaria root, and kanzo, liquorice) found that 26 (36%) recovered after simply stopping the medicine, while the rest needed immunosuppressive treatment, 13 (18%) received mechanical ventilation and 3 (4%) died. A 2025 systematic review of 37 cases of Kampo-related liver injury found 65.9% associated with Scutellaria root, with onset reported as within 45 days (range 1 to 730), and a clinic survey found liver injury in 4 of 37 outpatients (10.8%) who had blood tests on a Scutellaria-containing Kampo formula, all of whom recovered quickly after stopping it. The cited abstracts do not report a liver-injury case attributed to oren-gedoku-to by name. Mesenteric phlebosclerosis (a rare disease of the colon, described as thickening of the wall of the right colon with calcification of the mesenteric veins): a 2020 case report describes an 81-year-old woman admitted with right lower abdominal pain and high fever, whose CT scan showed thickening of the colon wall with linear calcifications and whose colonoscopy showed a dark-purple, swollen lining with erosions and ulcers; the disease was diagnosed on tissue examination, she stopped orengedokuto and was given antibiotics into a vein for a week, and six months later the colon lining had improved on colonoscopy although the ultrasound and CT scans showed no significant changes. That abstract does not say how long she had taken the formula. A 2012 report collected 4 of the authors' own patients, searched earlier reports for similar patients, and summarised 25 patients in all; 4 had taken orengedokuto, for a mean of 14.3 years, and only one ingredient, sansisi, was common to the herbal medicines of all 25. The abstract calls this crude drug geniposide in English and says it is a major constituent of Gardenia fruits, and the authors conclude that long-term use of geniposide in herbal medicines appears to be associated with the disease. In a 2014 study of 42 patients, about 90% of those the authors had treated reported a history of Chinese herbal medicine, particularly kamishoyosan, orengedokuto and sanshishi (given in that abstract as gardeniae fructus), and the authors say these findings suggest that the intake of Chinese herbal medicine, particularly sanshishi, is strongly associated with the disease. The Japanese national reports described above included 223 mesenteric phlebosclerosis events with prescription Kampo formulas (the abstract does not name this formula), which the authors say are believed to be caused by long-term use of Kampo formulas containing Gardeniae Fructus, and which rose markedly over the study period. A 2019 review lists the four herbs of Huang-Lian Jie-Du decoction as Rhizoma Coptidis, Radix Scutellariae, Cortex Phellodendri and 'Fructus Gradeniae' (spelled so in the abstract). These are case reports, associations and spontaneous reports, not proof that the formula caused the disease. On the other side, in a 2006 double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 265 people with accessory symptoms of high blood pressure, who took capsules of the formula's extract by mouth or placebo for 8 weeks, the overall safety rating did not differ significantly between the groups (251 people were included in the safety analysis; the abstract gives no event counts). A 2024 meta-analysis of 40 randomized trials (3,934 participants) of the decoction in type 2 diabetes, given alone or with other treatments, reported that it did not increase side effects, including diarrhoea, and a 2020 systematic review of 9 randomized trials (536 participants) of the formula in dyslipidaemia, under its Korean name Hwangryunhaedok-tang, found adverse events significantly less common when it was added to lipid-lowering drugs than with those drugs alone, and no serious adverse event was reported in the formula groups; most of that review's studies had a high risk of performance bias, and it rated the quality of evidence generally low. Platelets: in a 2006 study, the formula reduced platelet aggregation (clumping) in blood samples in the laboratory in a dose-dependent way, and in 10 patients with cerebral infarction (a type of stroke) who took it by mouth for up to 12 months, platelet aggregation fell significantly and spontaneous platelet activation was reduced (the abstract describes no comparison group for these 10 patients). In the laboratory, it did not significantly inhibit platelet activation triggered by added activating agents. The authors describe inhibition of platelet aggregation and activation at a clinically relevant dose. The abstract does not report bleeding, and no cited abstract tests the formula together with anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines. A 1991 laboratory study, which describes the formula as having haemostatic actions, also found that platelet aggregation rates fell significantly when plasma from healthy people and from patients was exposed to the formula in the laboratory, although the maximal aggregation time was shorter in the healthy people's plasma and longer in plasma from 8 of 20 patients with stroke (cerebrovascular accident); the abstract does not describe anyone taking the formula. Interactions (laboratory and animal data): extracts of Hwang-Ryun-Hae-Dok-Tang, a Korean spelling of the formula's name, strongly inhibited the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP1A2 and moderately inhibited CYP2C19, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 in human liver microsomes (a laboratory test), and in rats given the decoction extract by mouth for 14 days, blood levels of verapamil taken by mouth rose (24% higher AUC).
